# Probation Officers Want More Time for People, Not Paperwork


September 14, 2026


by Ashlin McMaken


##


Community supervision officers enter the profession to improve public safety and support people on their path toward meaningful change. Yet, their time and attention are consumed by the heavy administrative workload for hundreds of cases at any given time. They continue to balance desk-based activities like entering data, conducting risk assessments, meeting documentation requirements, and supporting program activities.


The question becomes whether an officer’s limited time is spent where it can have the greatest impact.


Polling results at the[American Probation and Parole Association (APPA) 2026 Summer Training Institute](https://www.appa-net.org/eweb/DynamicPage.aspx?webcode=Training-Institutes&site=APPA-3) surfaced this reality. Officers want more time for direct client interaction and less time managing paperwork and systems.


The poll results suggest that technology fragmentation is a significant part of the administrative burden, with officers chasing critical data across multiple systems every day. Officers spend significant time gathering and validating data before it can be used to support decision-making.


Conference attendees were also asked where they would spend their time if the administrative burden was lifted. Their responses centered on the core work of supervision: people and relationships.


Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a more active part of this conversation across agencies. Early perceptions of AI were often shaped by skepticism and concerns about replacement, but attitudes are shifting. Staff are viewing AI through a more practical lens. It has become a tool to support, not replace, officers.


This growing openness toward AI is present in the poll results. Last year, roughly 55% of poll respondents were excited or curious about AI. In 2026, that sentiment and comfort is 85%.


## What Practical AI Looks Like in Community Supervision


Officers do not need or want more technology simply for the sake of it. They need technology that reduces friction and fits naturally into daily work.


When information is easier to find and routine work can be completed faster within systems officers already use, agencies reclaim time to focus on the human side of supervision.


They spend less time searching for information and more time acting on it. AI helps make that possible.


- **Relevant information and insight retrieval.** Officers quickly know where to focus their day as AI helps organize and surface contextual support for each case, including what happened in a transfer case the day prior, what clients are at risk and why, or pattern recognition. Officers can review tailored, recommended actions for each case in a matter of minutes, not hours, and take appropriate next steps based on their own critical thinking skills.
- **Case note summarization and documentation assistance.** Officers can streamline routine documentation, making it more readable and professional for the courts. Based on real-time transcripts and audio notes, AI-generated and formatted case plan summaries cut through the noise and help officers identify deeper takeaways more quickly. For[California’s Placer County Probation Department](https://www.tylertech.com/resources/videos-and-webinars/placer-county-builds-ai-driven-probation-with-tyler) , the goal extended beyond reporting and to allow officers to take on more meaningful, client-facing work.


The grounding principle is straightforward: AI informs, but practitioners decide.


AI can assist with repetitive tasks and data synthesis, but officers remain in control. They are accountable for every decision, every relationship, and every interaction.


## Responsible AI: Why Trust and Human Oversight Matter


Community supervision agencies operate a complex environment shaped by public safety responsibilities, court requirements, and government compliance. Generic AI tools are not designed for the mission of government.


Agencies need technology purpose-built for community supervision workflows and systems officers already use. That's why embedded AI, built directly into existing case management systems, is best positioned to support the day-to-day reality of supervision. Efficiency is built into the workflow.


As agencies increasingly consider AI, they must balance this efficiency with[responsibility](https://www.tylertech.com/resources/resource-downloads/responsible-ai-in-community-supervision) . Clear policies, transparency, human-in-the-loop decision-making, data privacy, security safeguards, and human oversight establish the trust that is essential to sustaining operational value.


## Giving Time Back for the Work That Matters: Better Outcomes in Community Supervision


The poll results from the APPA 2026 Summer Training Institute highlight the disconnect between why people become supervision officers and how much of their time is consumed by administrative work.


The goal is not to automate community supervision. The goal is to preserve what community supervision is all about and create capacity for the work only practitioners can do.


Building relationships. Understanding changing circumstances. Exercising professional judgment. Supporting successful outcomes.


##### Responsible AI in Community Supervision


Calling on both vendors and agencies, these considerations describe design principles and responsible AI adoption.
